newsitem.title: BULGARIA: New Bulgarian parliament opens, pledges reform.
newsitem.headline: New Bulgarian parliament opens, pledges reform.

text.p: Bulgaria's new parliament held its first session on Wednesday, pledging long-delayed reforms to rescue the economy and to fight crime and corruption.

Elections held last month, after mass protests forced the fall of the former Socialist government in February, gave the centre-right Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) a big majority in the 240-seat assembly.
All parties in parliament have expressed support for the main points of the UDF's programme to bring the country out of crisis and into the European mainstream.

"Today, everyone is convinced that a new reformist majority has been born in Bulgaria and you here in parliament are the most important part of it because you are called upon to carry the burden of reforms on your shoulders," President Petar Stoyanov told the opening session.

"I trust that you will unite behind the national task, which is a solid legal base, structural reform, transparent privatisation, financial and bank stability, and the fight against crime in all its forms."
UDF supporters besieged and ransacked parliament on January 10 after the Socialists refused to vote on a UDF declaration proposing measures to bring the country out of crisis.
Since February, a caretaker cabinet appointed by Stoyanov has stabilised the national currency and brought bread and fuel shortages under control.

"The steps we have taken are in the right directions, the confidence of our trade partners and foreign investors is rekindling, and we hope that we can rely on their backing in our goals of European and Atlantic integration," Stoyanov said.
The April 19 election gave the UDF and its coalition allies 137 seats, and the Socialists 58.

Three smaller parties and coalitions are also represented -- the Alliance for National Salvation, which includes ethnic Turks and monarchists has 19 seats, the Euro-Left of Socialist dissidents 14, and the populist Bulgarian Business Bloc 12.

The UDF has nominated its leader Ivan Kostov as prime minister. His nomination must be approved by parliament and he will then appoint his cabinet, which is expected to include several figures from the interim cabinet.

Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Bozhkov is expected to retain the industry portfolio, overseeing reform of the unwieldy state sector, and Interior Minister Bogomil Bonev is expected to continue his fight against crime.

One of the first tasks of the new parliament will be to prepare introduction of a currency board, a restrictive fixed exchange rate mechanism prescribed by the International Monetary Fund to instil monetary discipline and restore confidence in the lev.

"We wish to restore the confidence of the Bulgarian people in our state institutions, the Bulgarian lev, Bulgarian banks, Bulgarian goods, as well as the confidence of foreign investors, international lending institutions, and foreign governments in our country," Kostov said.
